title: The Five Leadership Secrets You’re Not Supposed To Know
author: Gaurav Jain
summary: Drawing on more than twenty years of corporate leadership in software and tech, Gaurav Jain shares five lessons he says rarely appear in leadership training. First, leadership is more about people than strategy: a perfect plan is useless without the team's trust, as he learned when he pushed a platform change without consulting those who would implement it. Second, leaders will never have all the answers, and letting go of that expectation empowers the team and improves decisions. Third, leadership tests arrive in unexpected forms, such as managing egos and cross-divisional tension rather than timelines. Fourth and fifth, failure is inevitable but the response defines the leader, and the leader's job is to make heroes of others rather than take the spotlight, a point he illustrates with a credit-hoarding manager who drained his team.
points: A plan fails without the team's buy-in; Jain's unilateral platform change failed because the people implementing it were never consulted.
Trying to hold every answer created stress and distrust for Jain; letting go and inviting contributions was liberating for him and his team.
The hardest leadership tests are often interpersonal, such as managing egos and conflicting priorities across divisions, rather than project execution.
Being "protective" by hoarding information built a wall with his team; transparency made them stronger.
A manager who took credit for everything drained the team's motivation and ultimately hurt his own career, showing the leader's job is to make heroes of others.
quotes: But what I didn’t realize was that my team at the time wasn’t invested in my perfect plan. They didn’t care about the flowcharts or the grand vision—they cared about whether I listened to their ideas, whether I understood their struggles, and whether I cared about their growth.

Takeaway: You can have the best plan in the world, but if you don’t have your team’s trust and support, that plan is useless. Invest time in understanding your team, building their trust, and really getting to know what matters to them.

But the more I tried to get involved, the more stressed I felt. I was hesitant to tap into the knowledge of my team members, and that was not just adding to the lack of trust in the team, but creating more pressure on me to have the answers. I finally had to let go, and recognize that I didn’t know everything, and I didn’t NEED to know everything.

But what I didn’t expect was the tension between the different team managers. Each leader had a different perspective, different priorities, and different ways of working. Suddenly, I was not just managing the project—I was managing egos, conflicting ideas, and resistance to change.

As a leader, you will be tested in ways you never expected—through conflict, disagreement, and challenges to your authority. The true test of your leadership is how well you navigate those situations without succumbing to ego clashes and infights.

One of the biggest mistakes I made early on was trying to be “protective” of my team. I hoarded information and was not being transparent with my team about the challenges we faced. I was secretly justifying my behavior for shielding my team from the stress, but in reality, that only built a wall between me and my team.

I remember one of my managers who constantly wanted to take credit for everything the team did. Initially, I didn’t pay much attention to it, but when I realized what he was doing, my motivation to work hard and my energy started to drain. I started to feel unappreciated and suffocated.
